historical_evidence.finding: durable_branches=[]. Median net swing: CUT +0.36 (neg in 9%), TRANSITION +0.26 (21%), PULL_UP +0.09 (33%), PNR +0.04 (45%), SPOT_UP +0.02 (40%), POST_UP -0.22 (77%), DRIVE -0.27 (88%). n_units: CUT 103, DRIVE/POST_UP/SPO [cut]

4/8 PTs downstream real: CUT Ext 1.658 (supp +0.0220), TRANSITION 1.509 (+0.0145), SPOT_UP 1.303 (+0.0124), POST_UP 1.127 (+0.0194). DRIVE downstream not real (opp ATT +0.0024). Player downstream mostly BH ns except M. M [cut]

OTHER: 36% end in fouls, PPP inflated (FOUL_BUCKET). DRIVE: 12pp below foul benchmark (FOUL_LEAK). PNR shows 22% foul rate. Only 335 of 50,668 possessions (0.7%) map to a real play type via initiation_type.
Top recommendation changes in 40/104 = 38% units; DRIVE median net swing -0.27 (negative 88%), POST_UP -0.22 (77%).

Global horizons: DRIVE/SPOT_UP/TRANSITION=5; others 0 (PNR/CUT/POST_UP/PUTBACK). SPOT_UP lag-1 lift +0.027 ctrl_p=0.0000. Within-team: all horizons 0 except SPOT_UP horizon(all)=1; PNR lag-1 within_team_lift=-0.0218.
FAIL decay-sanity: DRIVE lifts +0.015,+0.020,+0.018,+0.021,+0.020 (flat). Within-team: DRIVE lag-1 +0.015 to -0.002. Cohen d ~0.01-0.03; p~0 from n>150k. Callable play-type horizons = 0.

failed_approaches.what_failed: 52-series sequential adaptation: durable pivot branches and net swing
failed_approaches.why: adequately powered null result; no conditional pivot branch met durability bar

failed_approaches.what_failed: Persistent Impact Score lag curves (own-sequence lags)
failed_approaches.why: artifact: flat non-decaying global lifts disappear after team-season demeaning; team-quality confound
artifact: flat non-decaying lifts, failure of decay-sanity, within-team baseline confound
artifact: OTHER foul inflation, DRIVE foul leakage, initiation_type mapping 0.7%

evidence_establishes: Opponent next-possession PPP after specific play types is measurable but effects are small (0.01-0.02 PPP) relative to direct PPP differences (FAM:SF-APPS-075).
Net swing (own PPP minus opponent next PPP) varies by play type, with DRIVE and POST_UP showing negative net swing (FAM:SF-APPS-049 descriptive).
Own-sequence lag effects are not real above team-quality confounding; within-team analysis shows no meaningful persistent impact except possibly SPOT_UP lag-1 (FAM:SF-APPS-073, FAM:SF-CHT-029).

Play-type labels suffer from significant artifacts: foul-related PPP inflation in OTHER, foul leakage in DRIVE, and only a tiny fraction of possessions map to a real play type via initiation_type (FAM:SF-CHT-025).
evidence_does_not_establish: Whether opponent next-PPP differences are causal or due to confounding (e.g., defensive rebounding, pace, opponent quality).
Whether the net swing magnitudes are stable across seasons or remain after controlling for game context.
Whether the play-type labeling quality can be improved or if current labels are sufficient for a rigorous test.
Whether own-sequence lags exist for any play type beyond SPOT_UP after controlling for score margin and other dynamic factors.
own_inferences: The question as posed likely overstates the potential for AVOID labeling; the existing evidence suggests opponent next-PPP effects are too small to justify AVOID labels that override direct efficiency, and own-sequence lags are artifacts of team-quality differences, not actionable.
A new test would likely reproduce these findings unless labeling methodology is substantially improved.
uncertainties: The magnitude of opponent next-PPP might be larger in specific game situations (e.g., late clock, particular matchups) not captured by average metrics; the net swing from SF-APPS-049 could be revisited with within-game controls.
The precise play-type definitions in the graph database are not fully specified (e.g., transition vs half-court handling).
The data for 2025-26 season includes partial records early and complete later, but the description confirms completeness for regular season and playoffs by the relevant dates.

historical_effect.explanation: Without the historical evidence, one might think the question is novel and testable; the archives show that own-sequence lags have been investigated and found to be artifacts, and opponent next-PPP effects are small and confounded. This leads to a recommendation not to proceed.

blocking_constraints.text: Play-type labeling quality is low (foul artifacts, initiation_type mapping only 0.7%), which undermines any analysis using derived play types.
Team quality and game state confound cross-possession effects (as shown in SF-APPS-073 and SF-CHT-029), requiring strong within-game controls that may still be insufficient.
Some play types (e.g., PUTBACK, POST_UP) have lower frequencies, reducing power for those categories.

prior_work.summary: Previous work has shown that own-sequence lag effects are artifactually driven by team quality, opponent next-PPP differences are small relative to direct PPP, and play-type labels contain significant foul-related artifacts and low mapping rates. Net swing estimates exist but have not been validated as causal or stable across seasons.

risks.text: Play-type labels derived from play-by-play have known fouling biases (OTHER inflated, DRIVE leakage) and only a small fraction of possessions map reliably.
Team strength, score margin, substitution patterns, and defensive matchups can create spurious associations between a play type and subsequent opponent scoring.
Low-frequency play types (e.g., POST_UP, PUTBACK) may have insufficient sample for precise estimation, especially after stratification.
Testing many play types and lag windows increases the risk of false positives if not accounted for.
Effect sizes of 0.01-0.02 PPP may require very large samples to detect with acceptable power, even with millions of possessions.
Misclassification of play types (e.g., lumping foul-related actions into OTHER) can distort both direct and lagged PPP estimates.

design.estimand: Average opponent next-possession points per possession (PPP) and own next-possession PPP following a half-court offensive play type X, conditional on game state and team/opponent fixed effects.
design.unit: One offensive possession by a team, with play type assigned from the graph database initiation_type (if mapping is improved).
design.sample: All NBA regular-season and playoff games from 2022-23 through 2025-26, excluding end-of-quarter possessions where the next possession starts a new quarter. For each play type, include only half-court possessions (no transition off makes unless defined separately).
design.power: With four full seasons (approximately 1 million+ possessions per common play type), a minimal detectable effect size of 0.015 PPP can be detected with >80% power at alpha=0.05/8 (corrected) if residual SD is ~0.3 PPP. However, the actual effect may be smaller.
design.controls: Fixed effects for team, opponent, and game ID; covariates for score margin (binned), period, time remaining, possession start type (made basket, dead ball, defensive rebound, offensive rebound), and home/away. Model opponent next-PPP residual from expected opponent offensive rating and defense.
design.falsification: Check that lag-1 effect is larger than lag-2 (decay) and that randomly permuting play types within games yields a null distribution. Also test within-team vs between-team comparisons to detect team-quality confound.
design.multiplicity: Apply Benjamini-Hochberg correction across the set of play types and the two outcomes (opponent next-PPP, own next-PPP).
design.decision_rule: A play type qualifies as 'AVOID'-worthy if the Bonferroni-corrected 95% confidence interval for opponent next-PPP lies entirely above 0.05 PPP (i.e., meaningful cost) and the effect passes falsification tests.
design.data_version: Derived play-type possession records from the NBA stats API graph database, as of 2026-06-19.

system_prompt:
You are a basketball analytics researcher deciding whether and how a research question should be studied.
You work only from the task statement and the tools listed below. Do not assume facts you have not seen.

The work has two stages, in this order.
Stage 1, retrieval:
1. Read the research objective and the data description.
2. Identify the research concepts and methodological questions the task raises.
3. Retrieve historical evidence by calling retrieve_history.
In stage 1 do not assess the question, predict outcomes or decide. Your only stage-1 reply is the retrieve_history call.
Stage 2, assessment, after the retrieval result is returned:
4. Summarise the relevant historical findings and failed approaches.
5. State what the historical evidence does and does not establish.
6. Assess whether the research question is testable.
7. Identify methodological risks and potential confounders.
8. Make the final research decision.
9. Explain whether and how the historical evidence changed the decision.
The stage-2 output format is given together with the retrieval result.

Evidence rules: keep what a retrieved record states (historical_evidence and failed_approaches, each citing the
identifier of a returned record and its status exactly as recorded) separate from your own inference and from
uncertainty or missing information. Cite only identifiers returned by a tool, and never describe an earlier study that
no tool returned. In some settings retrieval returns no records; then state that no historical evidence was available.

Tools:
- retrieve_history(research_concepts, methodological_questions, query): the prescribed retrieval step. Returns the most relevant consolidated study-family records of earlier research by this project that are available in this setting, with their identifiers; returns an empty list when none are available.
- glossary(): definitions of basketball and project terms used in task statements.
- data_catalog(): the fields available in each per-game data file.
- explore_graph(node_id): the relationships of one graph node (a family or a question, method, dataset, measure, limitation or risk node), with neighbour labels.
- read_family(id): the complete record of one study family (for example 'FAM:SF-APPA-001').

Protocol: every reply is exactly one JSON object and nothing else.
To call a tool: {"action": "tool", "tool": "<name>", "args": {...}}
To finish (stage 2 only): {"action": "final", "output": <object following the stage-2 schema>}
You may call at most 12 tools; then you must finish. Check that every opening brace has a closing brace.

Risk codes (use only these): SAMPLE_SIZE_POWER, EXPOSURE_SPARSITY, MEASURE_RELIABILITY, RTM_SELECTION, OUTCOME_DERIVED_LABEL, LEAKAGE_LOOKAHEAD, MECHANICAL_FLOOR, BASE_RATE, CONFOUNDING, LABEL_ERROR, PLACEBO_DEPENDENCE, MULTIPLE_TESTING, IMPLEMENTATION_BUG, DRIFT_NONSTATIONARITY

messages.content:
Research question (as posed on 2026-06-19, in the area of play-type labeling and data quality):
Opponent next-possession PPP after you run play X is large enough to drive AVOID labels; own-sequence lags similarly matter.

Data available on that date:
- NBA 2022-23 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2023-24 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2024-25 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2025-26 regular season (complete from 2026-04-13; partial before)
- NBA 2025-26 playoffs (complete from 2026-06-21; partial before)
- Sources: Per-game files from the NBA stats API: play-by-play (action type, sub-type, clock, period, score, player, shot distance and result), substitution rotation intervals, starters, defensive matchup minutes and partial possessions, box-score summary. Derived play-type possession records (initiator, play type, points) in a graph database built from the play-by-play.

Your job is to decide, before any analysis is run, whether this question can be answered with this data, what has already been established about it, which methodological and statistical risks threaten a test of it, and either a pre-registration-quality design or a reasoned recommendation not to proceed.

Stage 1. Reply only with the retrieval call: {"action": "tool", "tool": "retrieve_history", "args": {"research_concepts": ["..."], "methodological_questions": ["..."], "query": "..."}}

reasoning_details.text:
We are in Stage 1, so I need to retrieve historical evidence. The task is to evaluate the research question: "Opponent next-possession PPP after you run play X is large enough to drive AVOID labels; own-sequence lags similarly matter." 

First, I need to identify the research concepts and methodological questions. The question seems to relate to evaluating the impact of plays on subsequent opponent possessions (PPP) and whether those impacts are substantial enough to warrant "AVOID" labels (i.e., labeling a play as one to avoid). Also, it mentions own-sequence lags, meaning effects on the team's own next possessions.

I should break down the key concepts:
- Opponent next-possession PPP (points per possession) as an outcome.
- Play types (categorical labels like PnR, isolation, etc.) as the exposure.
- Lags (own and opponent subsequent possessions) indicating temporal sequence.
- The idea of "AVOID" labels, suggesting that if a play results in a negative outcome (like opponent scoring more), it might be flagged as a bad play to avoid. This could be a labeling decision problem (i.e., should we label a play as AVOID if it's followed by opponent scoring high?).
- The data includes play-by-play, player tracking, etc., with derived play-type possession records.
- The research likely relates to measuring the "on-court impact" of play types, possibly to build a labeling system for coaching decisions (like "avoid running this play because it leads to opponent fast breaks and scoring"). 

Methodological questions that arise:
- Causal inference: how to isolate the effect of one play type on subsequent possessions (opponent or own) given confounding by game context, score, opponent, lineup, etc.
- Temporal dependence: the structure of lags (immediate next possession vs. later). How far do the effects last?
- Data granularity: can we reliably link possessions and attribute outcomes (PPP) to previous plays?
- Measurement reliability: play type labels might be noisy. What's the reliability of derived play-type records?
- Sparsity: some play types are rare; sample size might be small.
- Risk of lookahead bias: if the labeling system uses future outcomes to label plays, but we need to test whether those outcomes are indeed predictive.
- Potential for regression to the mean, selection bias, etc.
- Whether PPP differences are large enough to be practically significant (driving AVOID labels).

So I'll craft the retrieval call with appropriate concepts and methodological questions. The query should combine the core ideas: opponent next-possession PPP after play types, own-sequence lags, AVOID labeling, etc.

Let's pick research concepts:
- "play-type possession outcomes"
- "opponent next-possession PPP"
- "AVOID labeling"
- "own-sequence lagged effects"

Methodological questions:
- "lagged possession-level causal effects"
- "play-type label reliability"
- "confounding in play-type evaluation"
- "temporal sequence modeling"

I'll make sure the call is concise.

Now, produce the JSON.

We need to proceed with stage 2. First, let's summarize the historical evidence and assess whether the question is testable. The user's task: "Opponent next-possession PPP after you run play X is large enough to drive AVOID labels; own-sequence lags similarly matter." The data: NBA 2022-23 to 2025-26 seasons and playoffs, per-game play-by-play, substitutions, starters, defensive matchups, box-score, derived play-type possession records (initiator, play type, points) in a graph database.

We have retrieval results with 10 study families. Let's parse them carefully.

First, we need to extract historical_evidence and failed_approaches citing the identifiers and status exactly as recorded. Also evidence_establishes, evidence_does_not_establish, own_inferences, uncertainties, historical_effect, testability, prior_work, risks, predicted_outcome, decision, design.

The research concepts: "play-type possession outcomes", "opponent next-possession PPP", "AVOID labeling", "own-sequence lagged effects". Methodological questions: lagged possession-level causal effects, play-type label reliability, confounding in play-type evaluation, temporal sequence modeling.

Now, from the retrieved records:

1. FAM:SF-APPS-049: "52-series sequential adaptation: durable pivot branches and net swing". Outcome: rejected. Finding: "durable_branches=[]. Median net swing: CUT +0.36 (neg in 9%), TRANSITION +0.26 (21%), PULL_UP +0.09 (33%), PNR +0.04 (45%), SPOT_UP +0.02 (40%), POST_UP -0.22 (77%), DRIVE -0.27 (88%). n_units: CUT 103, DRIVE/POST_UP/SPO [cut]...". Failure: "B_powered_null (adequately powered null result)" with evidence: "No conditional pivot branch met the durability bar (empty durable_branches). DRIVE/POST_UP negative net swing is the durable aftershock finding, recorded here as the positive half of the same run." Sample: 52 series, 104 units.

2. FAM:SF-APPS-075: "Extended Possession Value (direct PPP + opponent T+1 suppression)". Status: "not a hypothesis test". Finding: "4/8 PTs downstream real: CUT Ext 1.658 (supp +0.0220), TRANSITION 1.509 (+0.0145), SPOT_UP 1.303 (+0.0124), POST_UP 1.127 (+0.0194). DRIVE downstream not real (opp ATT +0.0024). Player downstream mostly BH ns except M. M [cut; read_family for full text]". Failure mechanism "E_unclear". Evidence: "Downstream effects are small (~0.01-0.02 PPP) relative to direct PPP gaps; player list is mostly non-FINDING after BH."

3. FAM:SF-CHT-025: "Play-type labeling audit: OTHER/DRIVE foul leakage". Status: "artifact". Finding: "OTHER: 36% end in fouls, PPP inflated (FOUL_BUCKET). DRIVE: 12pp below foul benchmark (FOUL_LEAK). PNR shows 22% foul rate. Only 335 of 50,668 possessions (0.7%) map to a real play type via initiation_type." Failure: "C_artifact (apparent effect produced by a construction, selection or labelling flaw)" with evidence about OTHER inflated, DRIVE 12pp below foul benchmark, initiation_type maps 0.7%. This indicates labeling quality issues.

4. FAM:SF-APPM-011: "Net-swing play-type scoring prototype". Status: "not a hypothesis test". Finding: "Top recommendation changes in 40/104 = 38% units; DRIVE median net swing -0.27 (negative 88%), POST_UP -0.22 (77%)." Failure: "E_unclear". Evidence: "Not evaluated against outcomes; uses in-series observed opp_next_PPP." Sample not recorded. Descriptive.

5. FAM:SF-APPS-073: "Persistent Impact Score lag curves (global then within-team)". Status: "artifact". Finding: "Global horizons: DRIVE/SPOT_UP/TRANSITION=5; others 0 (PNR/CUT/POST_UP/PUTBACK). SPOT_UP lag-1 lift +0.027 ctrl_p=0.0000. Within-team: all horizons 0 except SPOT_UP horizon(all)=1; PNR lag-1 within_team_lift=-0.0218." Failure: "C_artifact (apparent effect produced by a construction, selection or labelling flaw)" with evidence "Flat non-decaying global lifts disappear after team-season demeaning; remaining within-team memory is essentially none except SPOT_UP lag-1." Sample: DRIVE lag-1 n=163696; SPOT_UP n=175021. This is about own-sequence lags (action memory) directly relevant.

6. FAM:SF-CHT-029: "Persistent Impact Score Level 1 gate". Status: "artifact". Finding: "FAIL decay-sanity: DRIVE lifts +0.015,+0.020,+0.018,+0.021,+0.020 (flat). Within-team: DRIVE lag-1 +0.015 to -0.002. Cohen d ~0.01-0.03; p~0 from n>150k. Callable play-type horizons = 0." Failure: "C_artifact ... team-quality confound." Evidence about flat non-decaying lifts collapse under within-team baseline. Verdict: failed_gate. This is directly about own-sequence lags; shows that apparent positive lags are confounded by team quality.

7. FAM:SF07: "Sequential pair premium and defensive aftershock (8/8 PTs)". Status: "supported". Finding: "[APPA-049] A2 aftershock 8/8 PTs replicate all-games and playoffs (CUT +0.119 n=21,398 / PO +0.131 n=1,145 through TRANSITION +0.135 n=26,262 / +0.126 n=1,529). Top pair premiums: PUTBACK->TRANSITION +0.084 n=565; CUT->P [cut]". Failure: "D_positive (no failure: positive result)". Relationship: auto_limited_by LIM:small_sample. This is about defensive aftershock: opponent next-possession PPP after you run a certain play type? Wait: the description says "After the opponent runs play type X, the next offensive play type Y scores above Y's unconditional H2 baseline, and every PT has a defensive aftershock." That's about the opponent's play type affecting your next offense? Not directly our question. The question we have: "Opponent next-possession PPP after you run play X". That is the opponent's scoring after you run a play. That's a defensive aftershock of your offensive play. So FAM:SF07 might be relevant: "defensive aftershock (8/8 PTs)" means that after the opponent runs a play type, the next offensive play type scores above baseline, but it also says every PT has a defensive aftershock. Probably they measured opponent's next possession points after a given defensive play type? Need to read more. But the hitting mentions APPA-049 which we already have (the 52-series sequential adaptation with net swing). The SF07 result says "A2 aftershock 8/8 PTs replicate all-games and playoffs (CUT +0.119 n=21,398 / PO +0.131 n=1,145 through TRANSITION +0.135 n=26,262 / +0.126 n=1,529)". That appears to be positive defensive aftershock e.g. opponent's next possession PPP is higher after that PT? Actually, "aftershock" could mean the subsequent possession's offense efficiency for the same team, not opponent. Let's parse: the hypothesis "After the opponent runs play type X, the next offensive play type Y scores above Y's unconditional H2 baseline, and every PT has a defensive aftershock." So it's about opponent's play type influencing your next offense. That's reversed. However, the cell values like CUT +0.119 might be about your offense after opponent's CUT? Not our question. But they mention "defensive aftershock" which could be the opponent's next possession after you run a play type? I think the APPA-049 study (net swing) already incorporates opponent next-PPP. But I'll set aside SF07.

8. FAM:SF30: "Brown-initiated possession -> Tatum next-possession ATT". Status: "inconclusive". Finding about ATT estimates, CI crosses zero, signs flip. That's about specific player spillover, not play type. Not directly relevant.

9. FAM:SF-APPA-050: "Superstar sequential suppression: opponent play before the star". Status: "not a hypothesis test". Finding: opponent play type suppressing star's next-possession PPP. Sample with small n_after (32-95). Risks DRIFT_NONSTATIONARITY. Not our direction but shows that opponent's prior play type may affect star's PPP, but not our own play type.

10. FAM:SF-APPM-022: "Superstar suppression profiles (incl. Q5c sequential triggering)". Status: "inconclusive". Similar direction, not directly about own play type opponent next PPP.

Now, the central question: "Opponent next-possession PPP after you run play X is large enough to drive AVOID labels; own-sequence lags similarly matter." So we need to test two things: (1) whether opponent next-possession PPP after a team runs play type X is sufficiently large and negative (or positive) to warrant labeling that play type as AVOID (i.e., the opponent scores more after we run that play, making it undesirable); (2) own-sequence lags similarly matter, i.e., running play X affects your own subsequent possessions.

The historical evidence directly addresses these:

- For opponent next-PPP after play X: FAM:SF-APPS-049 (rejected) showed net swing (own PPP - opponent next PPP) by play type, and DRIVE and POST_UP had negative net swing (opponent outscored you next possession), while CUT and TRANSITION had positive net swing. But the failure was that no conditional pivot branch met durability bar (empty durable_branches). However, the net swing magnitude by PT was large: CUT +0.36, TRANSITION +0.26, etc., DRIVE -0.27. That suggests opponent next-PPP differences might be large enough for AVOID labeling. But the study was about "durable pivot branches" being rejected, not about whether the effect size is large enough. The question is about effect magnitude driving AVOID labels, not about pivot branches. The net swing findings are relevant, but the study's overall outcome was rejected for the hypothesis of durable pivot branches, not the descriptive net swing. Still, we can use the net swing estimates as prior evidence that some PTs have large opponent next-PPP effects. However, we need to consider confounds and labeling artifacts.

- FAM:SF-APPS-075: Extended Possession Value found downstream opponent PPP suppression small (~0.01-0.02) relative to direct PPP gaps. That suggests opponent next-PPP effects may be too small to drive AVOID labels, but it's considering "downstream" as opponent's possession T+1? They say "direct PPP + opponent T+1 suppression". They found 4/8 PTs downstream real, but effect sizes are tiny (~0.01-0.02). So the opponent next-PPP difference might be only 0.01-0.02, which may not be "large enough" to drive avoid labels.

- FAM:SF-CHT-025: labeling audit shows significant artifact: OTHER inflated, DRIVE foul leakage, initiation_type mapping only 0.7% of possessions. This suggests that the play-type labels themselves have quality issues, which could confound any analysis of play-type effects on opponent next-PPP. So the derived play-type possession records may be unreliable.

- For own-sequence lags: FAM:SF-APPS-073 (artifact) and FAM:SF-CHT-029 (artifact) robustly show that apparent cross-possession memory (own team PPP after running a play type) is an artifact of team-quality confounding; within-team demeaning eliminates most effects, leaving only SPOT_UP lag-1 maybe. So own-sequence lags do not seem to exist meaningfully. So the claim that "own-sequence lags similarly matter" is likely false; the historical evidence strongly suggests they are artifact. That part of the question is unlikely to hold.

So overall, the question as posed (both factors large enough to drive AVOID labels) seems undermined given the small opponent next-PPP effects (per SF-APPS-075), the net swing from SF-APPS-049 might be driven by defensive rebound/pace confounds rather than causal opponent suppression, and own-sequence lags are likely confounded artifacts.

Now, we need to assess testability. Data: NBA 2022-23 through 2025-26 with full seasons, play-by-play. That's rich. We can theoretically compute opponent's next possession PPP after a given play type, and own next possessions. But we need to account for many confounders: game state, score margin, time, opponent strength, home/away, fatigue, lineup, etc. The historical work shows that team-quality confounding is a major issue for cross-possession analyses, and that within-team or within-game controls may be needed. Also, the play-type labels may be noisy, and only a small fraction of possessions may be cleanly labeled (per CHT-025). The initiation_type mapping is weak. So the data quality might limit power.

Power: we can estimate sample sizes. For opponent next-PPP, we might have thousands of possessions per play type per season. For own lags, similarly. But the effects might be small, so we need large N to detect. However, p-testable might be moderate if we use appropriate controls. But the prior artifact findings suggest that naive analysis will produce spurious results.

Given the historical evidence, we should consider the following risks: CONFOUNDING (team quality, game state), MEASURE_RELIABILITY (play-type labeling), EXPOSURE_SPARSITY (rare play types may have low sample for some combos), SAMPLE_SIZE_POWER (small net swing differential and low n for some PTs), LABEL_ERROR (misclassification), RTM_SELECTION (regression to mean from selecting extreme sequences), LEAKAGE_LOOKAHEAD (using future possession to define play type?), MULTIPLE_TESTING (testing many PTs). Also MECHANICAL_FLOOR: not likely. OUTCOME_DERIVED_LABEL: play type labels may be derived from the same possession's outcome? Not sure. But labeling based on action types may be post-hoc, not prerecorded, but it's from play-by-play, so likely independent. However, the artifact found in CHT-025 suggests PPP differences are due to fouls, not true efficiency, which is a label error.

We should design a test: Use within-team, within-game comparisons to control for team strength, opponent, game context. For each play type, compare opponent next-possession PPP to a suitable baseline (e.g., opponent next-PPP after a random stoppage or after other play types, conditional on the same game state variables). Use mixed-effects or fixed effects regressions. But the own-sequence lags likely will be null after proper controls. The opponent next-PPP might also shrink.
